questions.question: A 45-year-old patient with two children wants contraception. She smokes a pack of cigarettes a day and takes lisinopril for hypertension. She wants to keep having a monthly period. Which method is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Smoking over age 35 and hypertension both contraindicate estrogen-containing contraception.
explanations.B: The copper IUD has no hormones, is more than 99% effective, and preserves monthly menses, which meets all of her needs.
explanations.C: The implant is effective and estrogen-free but causes unpredictable, irregular bleeding rather than monthly periods.
explanations.D: The LNG IUD suppresses the endometrium and often causes amenorrhea or irregular bleeding.
explanations.E: DMPA causes amenorrhea in 40–50% of users at 1 year and irregular bleeding before that.

questions.question: A 30-year-old patient with one child has no medical problems. She missed her period, and ultrasound shows an intrauterine pregnancy of 8 weeks' gestation. She requests medication abortion. Labs are shown. What is the most appropriate response?

answers.A: Decline, because gestation exceeds the limit
answers.B: Decline, because her hemoglobin is too low

explanations.A: Medication abortion is available up to 10 weeks (70 days), and she is at 8 weeks.
explanations.B: Anemia contraindicates medication abortion only when hemoglobin is below 9.0 g/dL; 10.5 g/dL is acceptable.
explanations.C: She is within 10 weeks with no contraindication, so mifepristone 200 mg followed 24–48 h later by buccal misoprostol 800 mcg is appropriate.
explanations.D: Misoprostol alone is an alternative regimen; with no contraindication to mifepristone, the combination is preferred.
explanations.E: She is also a good candidate for procedural abortion, but nothing limits her to it.

questions.question: A 24-year-old patient had unprotected intercourse 2 days ago and wants to prevent pregnancy. Her BMI is 36 kg/m². Which option is the most effective emergency contraception for her?

explanations.A: The Yuzpe regimen is rarely used, less effective (about 75% reduction) and has more side effects.
explanations.B: An IUD placed within 5 days is the most effective emergency contraception and works at any weight.
explanations.C: Plan B is less effective with BMI over 30.
explanations.D: A daily progestin-only pill is not an emergency contraceptive.
explanations.E: Ulipristal is the most effective EC pill but is less effective with BMI over 35.

questions.question: A 19-year-old patient had unprotected intercourse 4 days ago and wants an oral emergency contraceptive. Her BMI is 24 kg/m². She does not want an IUD. Which option is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Yuzpe is less effective and has more side effects than the other EC pills.
explanations.B: Levonorgestrel is labeled for use within 3 days, and she is at day 4.
explanations.C: Mifepristone is used for medication abortion, not emergency contraception.
explanations.D: Misoprostol causes uterine contractions for abortion, not emergency contraception.
explanations.E: Ulipristal works up to 5 days after intercourse and is equally effective on days 1 and 5.

questions.question: A 28-year-old patient asks how levonorgestrel emergency contraception works, because she is worried it causes an abortion. Which statement is most accurate?

answers.A: It blocks implantation of a fertilized egg
answers.B: It causes shedding of an implanted embryo
answers.D: It kills sperm in the uterine cavity
answers.E: It prevents the LH surge and delays ovulation

explanations.A: EC does not appear to inhibit implantation.
explanations.B: EC does not interrupt or affect an established pregnancy and is not an abortifacient.
explanations.C: Uterine contractions are misoprostol's effect, not levonorgestrel's.
explanations.D: Killing sperm and inhibiting tubal motility is how the copper IUD works as EC.
explanations.E: Oral EC prevents the LH surge, which delays or inhibits ovulation so fertilization does not occur.

questions.question: A 26-year-old patient on a combined oral contraceptive has spotting on days 4–8 of each pack. She takes her pills consistently. Which change is most likely to help?

explanations.A: Lowering estrogen would worsen early-cycle bleeding, which already reflects too little estrogen.
explanations.B: Early-cycle (days 1–9) breakthrough bleeding reflects estrogen deficiency, so more estrogen should stabilize the endometrium.
explanations.C: Late-cycle (days 10–21) breakthrough bleeding is the sign of progestin deficiency.
explanations.D: Progestin-only pills have a variable bleeding profile and would not fix this.
explanations.E: Continuous placebo makes no pharmacologic sense and would leave her unprotected.

questions.question: A 33-year-old patient started a combined oral contraceptive 3 months ago. She reports breast tenderness, nausea, bloating and headaches that started with the pill. Which adjustment best addresses her symptoms?

explanations.A: Adding progestin does not address estrogen-excess symptoms.
explanations.B: Nausea, breast tenderness, headaches and fluid retention are signs of estrogen excess.
explanations.C: Progestin excess causes increased appetite, acne, hirsutism and mood changes, not these symptoms.
explanations.D: More estrogen would worsen these estrogen-excess symptoms.
explanations.E: More progestin would add progestin side effects without fixing estrogen excess.

questions.question: A 27-year-old patient with migraines wants combined hormonal contraception. Before her headaches, she sees flashing zigzag lines for about 20 minutes. She does not smoke and her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Which mechanism underlies the main concern with combined hormonal contraception in her?

answers.A: Decreased SHBG and increased free testosterone
answers.B: Increased factors V, VIII and X and fibrinogen
answers.E: Suppression of the midcycle LH surge

explanations.A: Combined OCs increase SHBG and lower free testosterone, which is a benefit.
explanations.B: Estrogen raises procoagulant factors (V, VIII, X, fibrinogen) and lowers anticoagulants; with migraine with aura, the stroke risk makes estrogen contraindicated.
explanations.C: First-pass metabolism affects oral drug levels, not her stroke risk.
explanations.D: Increased PR concentration lets a lower progestin dose work; it is not a safety concern.
explanations.E: LH surge suppression is how the method works, not why it is dangerous for her.

questions.question: A 25-year-old patient with acne and mild hirsutism starts a combined oral contraceptive. After 6 months her skin has improved. Which hormonal change best explains this?

answers.A: Decreased hepatic SHBG and less ovarian androgen
answers.B: Decreased hepatic SHBG and more ovarian androgen
answers.C: Increased hepatic SHBG and less ovarian androgen
answers.D: Increased hepatic SHBG and more ovarian androgen
answers.E: Unchanged SHBG and blocked androgen receptors

explanations.A: Lower SHBG would raise free testosterone and worsen acne.
explanations.B: Both changes would raise free androgens.
explanations.C: Combined OCs increase liver SHBG and suppress LH-driven ovarian testosterone, lowering free testosterone; the progestin also inhibits 5α-reductase.
explanations.D: More ovarian androgen would offset any SHBG benefit, and the pill suppresses ovarian androgen.
explanations.E: Combined OCs work through SHBG and less androgen synthesis, not by blocking androgen receptors.

questions.question: A 22-year-old patient wants contraception that lasts several years without daily attention. She is told the device is more than 99% effective, lasts 3–5 years, and is inserted in the upper inner arm. After insertion, which side effect is most likely?

explanations.A: Hyperkalemia is a caution with drospirenone, which is spironolactone-derived.
explanations.B: The implant does not suppress SHBG to cause acne.
explanations.C: The etonogestrel implant's main disadvantage is unpredictable, irregular bleeding.
explanations.D: Heavier, crampier periods are typical of the copper IUD.
explanations.E: DMPA is the only contraceptive associated with weight gain.

questions.question: A 17-year-old patient has received depot medroxyprogesterone acetate every 3 months for 2 years. She has not had a period in 14 months and has gained 5 kg. A DXA scan shows reduced bone density. Which statement about her bone loss is most accurate?

answers.A: It is caused by a direct toxic effect on osteoblasts
answers.B: It is due to hyperestrogenism and is permanent
answers.C: It is due to hypoestrogenism and is reversible
answers.D: It is due to secondary hyperparathyroidism
answers.E: It is unrelated to the medication

explanations.A: DMPA is not directly toxic to osteoblasts.
explanations.B: DMPA lowers estrogen, and the bone loss is transient.
explanations.C: DMPA suppresses ovulation and estrogen, causing transient, reversible bone mineral density loss.
explanations.D: Hyperparathyroidism is not the mechanism.
explanations.E: Bone density loss is a known DMPA side effect.

questions.question: A 29-year-old patient with lupus and a history of DVT wants a daily pill. She is started on a norethindrone 0.35 mg pill. Which counseling point is most important for its effectiveness?

answers.A: Skip pills during the fourth week each month
answers.B: Take it at the same time daily, within 3 hours
answers.C: Take it with a high-fat meal for absorption
answers.D: Take it within 24 hours of the usual time
answers.E: Use it only on days of intercourse

explanations.A: Progestin-only pills are taken continuously with no hormone-free week.
explanations.B: Norethindrone works mainly by thickening cervical mucus and must be taken within a 3-hour window or effectiveness drops.
explanations.C: There is no food requirement.
explanations.D: A 24-hour window applies to the drospirenone pill, not norethindrone.
explanations.E: It is a daily method, not coitus-dependent.

questions.question: A 36-year-old patient with chronic kidney disease (creatinine 2.1 mg/dL) who takes lisinopril wants an estrogen-free daily pill with a forgiving dosing window. A drospirenone 4 mg pill is being considered. Which laboratory value most warrants monitoring?

explanations.A: Drospirenone does not affect calcium.
explanations.B: Glucose monitoring is not a drospirenone concern.
explanations.C: Hemoglobin matters before medication abortion, not with drospirenone.
explanations.D: Drospirenone is derived from spironolactone and can cause hyperkalemia, especially with CKD and an ACE inhibitor.
explanations.E: Sodium is not the key concern.

questions.question: A 34-year-old patient with heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea wants long-acting contraception that will also lighten her periods. She has a levonorgestrel IUD placed. Which mechanism does this device NOT use?

explanations.A: Endometrial atrophy is part of its effect and explains the lighter bleeding.
explanations.B: The LNG IUD acts locally and does not inhibit ovulation, unlike the implant and DMPA.
explanations.C: It inhibits sperm motility and function.
explanations.D: Its mechanism is a local progestin effect.
explanations.E: It thickens cervical mucus, keeping sperm from the upper tract.

questions.question: A 31-year-old patient with Wilson disease wants a long-acting, reversible intrauterine method. Which device is contraindicated?

explanations.A: Kyleena is a levonorgestrel IUD and has no copper.
explanations.B: Liletta is a levonorgestrel IUD.
explanations.C: Mirena is a levonorgestrel IUD.
explanations.D: ParaGard is the copper IUD, which is contraindicated with Wilson disease or copper allergy.
explanations.E: Skyla is a levonorgestrel IUD.

questions.question: A 23-year-old patient weighing 105 kg (BMI 34) wants a weekly contraceptive patch. Which counseling point is most accurate?

answers.A: Both patches are less effective at her weight
answers.B: Both patches avoid all estrogen side effects
answers.D: The levonorgestrel patch is preferred at her BMI
answers.E: The norelgestromin patch lowers estrogen exposure

explanations.A: The norelgestromin patch is less effective above about 90 kg, and the levonorgestrel patch is not approved for BMI over 30.
explanations.B: The norelgestromin patch's estrogen exposure is 60% higher than a 35 mcg pill, possibly raising VTE risk.
explanations.C: Patches avoid first-pass metabolism by delivering hormone continuously to the systemic circulation.
explanations.D: The levonorgestrel patch is not approved for BMI over 30, with lower efficacy and higher DVT risk.
explanations.E: The norelgestromin patch raises estrogen exposure (AUC) compared with a pill.

questions.question: A 27-year-old patient stopped her combined oral contraceptive because of nausea. She wants an estrogen-containing method with the lowest estrogen dose, no nausea, and the least breakthrough bleeding, and she does not want to remember a daily or weekly step. Which method best fits?

explanations.A: Oral pills undergo first-pass metabolism, which can cause nausea, and must be taken daily.
explanations.B: Patches must be changed weekly.
explanations.C: The monthly ring (EE + etonogestrel) gives a low, continuous estrogen dose with no first-pass metabolism, no nausea and less breakthrough bleeding.
explanations.D: The norelgestromin patch gives higher estrogen exposure than a pill and is changed weekly.
explanations.E: A triphasic pill is still daily and oral.

questions.question: A 26-year-old patient takes mifepristone 200 mg orally for a medication abortion at 7 weeks. Thirty-six hours later she takes a second drug buccally and develops cramping, bleeding, nausea, diarrhea and a low-grade fever. What is the mechanism of the second drug?

explanations.A: No ER antagonist is part of the medication abortion regimen.
explanations.B: Oxytocin is not part of the medication abortion regimen.
explanations.C: PR blockade describes the first drug, mifepristone.
explanations.D: Misoprostol is a PGE1 analog that causes uterine contractions and cervical dilation; GI upset, fever and cramping are its side effects.
explanations.E: Blocking a prostaglandin receptor would reduce, not cause, uterine contractions.

questions.question: A 30-year-old patient requests medication abortion at 6 weeks. She has had Addison disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) for 4 years and takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Hemoglobin is 12.4 g/dL. What is the most appropriate response?

answers.A: Mifepristone is contraindicated; consider other options
answers.B: Proceed after doubling the misoprostol dose
answers.C: Proceed after holding hydrocortisone for 48 hours
answers.D: Proceed after transfusion to raise hemoglobin

explanations.A: Mifepristone also blocks glucocorticoid receptors, so in chronic adrenal failure or long-term steroid therapy it risks acute adrenal insufficiency; both are label contraindications.
explanations.B: Changing the misoprostol dose does not remove the contraindication.
explanations.C: Holding steroid replacement in adrenal insufficiency risks adrenal crisis.
explanations.D: Her hemoglobin is above the 9.0 g/dL threshold; anemia is not the problem.
explanations.E: Her adrenal failure is a listed contraindication, so standard dosing is not appropriate.

questions.question: A 25-year-old patient is choosing among methods based on their mechanism. Her clinician explains that one method releases ions into the uterus, producing a sterile inflammatory reaction that is spermicidal and decreases tubal motility, and that it can also be used as emergency contraception. How long is this method FDA-approved?

explanations.A: Three years is the duration of Skyla and the implant's FDA approval.
explanations.B: Five years is Kyleena's duration and the implant's effective duration.
explanations.C: Eight years is the duration of the 52 mg LNG IUDs (Mirena, Liletta).
explanations.D: The copper IUD is FDA-approved for 10 years.
explanations.E: Clinical data support 12 years of copper IUD use, but FDA approval is for 10.
